title: Archimedes floating-body equilibrium constructor with fluid-state transitions
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED, NOT SELECTED. Archimedes On Floating Bodies I begins from a fluid-pressure postulate, derives the spherical surface of a resting fluid, and continues to floating-body equilibrium and stability. The same body/fluid argument must preserve density, submerged portion, and vertical equilibrium; a boundary change produces a different state.

source.work: Archimedes, On Floating Bodies, Book I
source.source_span: Postulate 1; Propositions 1–2 on a spherical resting-fluid surface; later Book I floating-body equilibrium propositions
source_facts: The postulate relates pressure among continuous fluid parts.
Propositions 1–2 derive the spherical surface of a fluid at rest around the earth's centre.
The book applies fluid equilibrium to floating bodies and distinguishes equilibrium position/stability from mere presence in fluid.

duplicate_screen.checked: ideas search/duplicates Archimedes floating/equilibrium and route-check geometry/physical state; prior reflection/arithmetic cards inspected
duplicate_screen.difference: This is a fluid-state and stability constructor with a shared body/fluid argument, not a reflection composition, compass construction, or numerical quantity decoder.

worked_examples: a changed submerged portion changes the balance state; a stable orientation is not identical to any floating position
constructor.consequence: Changing the body/fluid or submerged-portion argument changes the equilibrium/stability output while retaining the same pressure operator. A presence-only rival predicts one generic FLOAT result and cannot distinguish stable equilibrium from an arbitrary immersion.
constructor.smallest_test: Require two complete source passages or propositions sharing the pressure/equilibrium operator but changing body/fluid or submerged state, with a predicted stable/unstable contrast.
constructor.rival: A static geometry catalogue in which circles, bodies and water are listed independently and no state transition links pressure to equilibrium.
